review_text:
A few years ago I wrote a book about the trials and tribulations of the Dutch colonial army of the former Dutch East Indies (KNIL) and the Australian commandos against the Imperial Japanese Army during WWII on Timor. This was requested by daughters and sons of these Dutch (which includes many people with Indonesian roots) veterans. A friend of mine persuaded me to visit Timor and all these places. So we went this summer, for which I'm very grateful to him. But where to start? This certain part of history was all so very specific. Manny Timor Tours was the only company that made a specific itinerary about WWII (including the lesser known Dutch participation) on the entire island of Timor. And it was also their first time - my compliments.

We had Serafim as our guide, a very nice and accessible man that really made our trip. He knows six forms of Tetum and endlessly translated for us, which truly enhanced our experience of the history of Timor, having many conversations with elderly Timorese about WWII, the Portuguese colonisation and the Indonesian occupation and subsequent chaos and massacres. It was emotional, but Serafim really did well. He was also very flexible in his time schedule, so nothing is super 'fixed'. If you book with Manny Timor Tours, request Serafim. And finally, he is a good driver - and believe me - that is no unnecessary luxury on Timor! The island is beautiful, but some roads are quite hard to navigate and a good driver really makes the difference.

When you go of the beaten track, do not expect any Western luxuries, but you have to embrace this. Many Timor Tours tries its utmost best to make you as comfortable as possible. Be it a good car or a good accommodation. Timor-Leste is a new nation, not even 20 years have passed since the last big troubles. Be nice and respectful towards a nation that is building its nationhood and has known more massacres in the last 25 years than we can name. The Timorese are very friendly and if you love unspoiled nature, this is your spot. And if you're interested in the WWII history of Timor, Manny Timor Tours is the company for you. They took us all around the island, from Díli to Ataúro island, Viqueque, Tutuala and unspoiled Jaco island in the east, Atambua, Soe and Kupang in the west. No place is too far. Also, don't repeat my mistake by focusing to much on the Portuguese language, as it is rarely spoken anymore. Tetum and Indonesian are the languages to go on Timor! And the international language is English now, not Portuguese anymore.

Have fun and enjoy this extraordinary island.

review_text:
I spent ten days on a tour with Manny Timor Tours. It first started by contacting the agency  to customise the tour. Lito, and then Erin, were very responsive and helpful. In the end, we decided to take bits and pieces of existing packages and ended up with a tour starting from Dili, going the to Mount Ramelau, Suai in the Southern Coast, Same, Betano, Viqueque, Ossù, Mondo Perdido, Veniliale, Baucau, Los Palos, Tutuala, Jaco Island, Com and then back to Dili through Baucau. This tour was a good mix between hiking, including the ascent of Mount Ramelau to see the wonderful sunrise, beach activities, and history, from the Portuguese colony to the Japanese attacks during WWII and, more recently, the massacres related to the Indonesian occupation.

Alex, my guide was very friendly and knowledgeable, particularly of the history during the occupation times. In addition to fully following the programme, he also sometimes went for the extra-mile, for example when we visited one of his friends’ farm in Los Palos. Alex is also knowledgeable about coffee and knows all the coffee-shops of Timor-Leste, and it was great to stop at the best ones to enjoy a good coffee and take a break from the (often) bumpy roads. In addition, Alex was a very safe driver and our 4x4 vehicle was robust enough to cross rivers when bridges were damaged.

So this was a remarkable experience, off the beaten tracks, particularly between Suai and Tutuala, where we did not meet any tourist at all.

As a consequence, one should be aware that while such a tour has its price (mainly because the local currency is the US dollar), the local standards may not be those regularly met in more touristic countries, particularly in the most remote areas that this tour allowed me to visit. The accommodation were clean and decent, but sometimes with no hot water and not always with en-suite bathrooms. So, if you are looking forward to relaxing in a jacuzzi with a glass of champagne after a busy hiking day, Timor-Leste may not be your place. Also, do not expect to have lunch at a fixed time, simply because, in some areas, you can spend hours on the road without seeing a decent place to have some food. Please also note that the roads can be unpredictable because of landslides or broken bridges. We made it every time but this may not always be the case.

So, be prepared for the adventure! At least Timor-Leste is still one of those countries allowing for it, while being a very friendly and safe country. With Many Timor Tours, you will feel safe and in good hands for enjoying this adventure.

review_text:
A museum you must visit when you come to Timor-Leste.
When we talk about genocide, our minds often jump straight to Europe. But traveling through Southeast Asia, I’ve repeatedly come across stories of occupation and genocide from the eastern side of the world—stories that are just as brutal, just as important, and far less spoken about.
Timor-Leste is a newly independent Asian nation that lived through decades of occupation under different regimes. The trauma here runs deep—woven through families, carried across generations. This museum stands as a quiet but powerful reminder of the ugly reality of colonialism, war, and genocide.
What makes the experience truly human, though, are the guides.
The people who walk you through the exhibitions are not just historians—they are witnesses. Many of them lived through the occupation themselves, while also carrying stories passed down from their parents and grandparents. They bridge the gaps between dates, events, and photographs, helping you connect the incidents in a way books never can.
It is a testimony to human endurance and strength—to return every day and tell stories of resistance, loss, and survival. To educate others about the occupation, not as distant history, but as lived reality.
Listening to them, you begin to understand the true gravity of what happened—what was lost, what was endured, and how easily we take life for granted.
And yet… what stays with me the most is the people outside the museum.
Everyone smiles.
They want to know where you’re from.
Their favorite Bollywood movie is Kuch Kuch Hota Hai—and they love talking about it.
There is caution, of course (and that’s understandable). But there is also warmth, curiosity, and resilience.
This country humbles you in ways you don’t expect.
It makes you slow down.
It makes you appreciate what you have.
And for that, I’m truly grateful to be here

We stopped by Pousada de Maubisse for a lunch break on our way up to Mount Ramelau or Tatamailau (local language means Grandfather of all) is the highest mountain in Timor Leste and also Timor Island. It is a rest house located in Maubisse, which is the pass over before going to Hato Bulico where we would start our climb. It could be an option for staying overnight if you want to spend more time exploring Maubisse at that time, currently I believe it's under renovation.

It was a tranquil experience for us as no one was around. When we entered the place, there were two rows of rooms on both sides. After that we would pass by a garden with surrounding 360 view before we entered the big house. There was a rustic fire place in the living room, or maybe more suitable to be called dining room. The place was empty and cold when no one was around. The fire place was nice; the whole space was spacious but quite old. We saw a sitting room with two stretch of long sofa, there was a clean toilet with full big bucket of water and a lot of toilet papers.

The food was simple and good, but took very long to prepare. On our way back from the climbing the next day, we ordered before we started the descent and yet we needed to wait for another two hours. I assumed they cooked with fire wood that was why it took much longer but it was good.

It's very nice climb overall and the stopover at Pousada de Maubisse is very memorable. We had the place all for ourselves and it's a nice, quiet, gorgeous, and peaceful time there.

review_text:
Should be visited with a local guide (which your accommodation should be able to arrange), as it is a sacred place and is unmarked from the main road. Ili Kere Kere is $10 per person.

Ili Kere Kere is reached by a rough road off the main road between Tutuala and Valu Beach, followed by a 2.3km return walk (not the 250m denoted by the signage at the start of the trail). This walk gets increasingly rough and steep (downhill) before reaching the best known rock art depicting a sea urchin, as well as a harder to recognise image of cockfighting. Walking around the base of the cliff offers great views of Jaco Island in the distance. Allow about an hour to visit Ili Kere Kere. Look out for the giant bee hives hanging from the rock overhang above the rock art.

From where the trail to Ili Kere Kere starts there are two other trails that are far less visited. Pati-Patinu (500m walk apparently) goes to seven holes in stone, which demonstrate a tradition practice by ancestors of the Tutuala area. Moa Mimiraka (700m walk) is home to four pieces of rock art illustrating headhunting, arm stencil, a festive event, and warriors.

This time we stayed for two nights, one in the dorm and one in the Blue Room. Both were simple but comfortable, with fans and plenty of power outlets. I love the natural scent from the dried leaves used for the roof because it feels so close to nature. I especially loved the open roof toilet. It is such a unique experience that made me feel immersed in the outdoors.

Breakfast with homemade bread, marmalade, and Timor coffee. Meals can be arranged in advance, and every dish is freshly cooked, I liked grilled fish a lot.

All guests staying there joined whale watching trips for first day and made it for two days eventually. It was great going with local fishing boats that move gently with smaller engines. The fishermen were very professional at spotting whales and keeping a respectful distance. We spotted sperm whales, with four boats joining the expedition. It was truly unforgettable.

Apesar de já conhecer o Fernando Madeira há vários anos, nunca tinha tido a oportunidade de visitar o espaço daTerra em Baucau.
Desta vez proporcionou-se e foi uma experiência muito boa. Fiquei, com os meus 3 filhos, num bungalow para 4 pessoas.

Decidimos ficar duas noites, a caminho entre Díli e a ponta leste da ilha (onde fomos visitar Jaco). É uma excelente opção, para tornar esse trajeto mais fácil (de Dili a Baucau são 2 horas de carro, com a estrada toda em muito boas condições).

O alojamento, a comida e o serviço são fantásticos. O acesso pode ser um bocadinho complicado dependendo do tipo de carro que se use (um carro citadino terá alguma dificuldade em aceder à última parte do percurso), mas em geral só temos a dizer bem.

Todo o conceito é de quinta ecológica, inserida no meio da natureza, mas muito bem ajustada ao conforto de quem quer descansar e usufruir de uns dias em paz.

As casa de banho são comunitárias, mas há várias e com um nível de conforto que eu não imaginava sequer encontrar ali.

Muito bom!

It's an ideal spot for photography, a short walk, or simply to appreciate a quieter side of Aileu.

My husband and I recently had the most incredible experience at Balibo Fort Hotel, celebrating both my birthday and our first wedding anniversary. Under the new management of Pelikan Paradise, the hotel has truly elevated its hospitality, making our stay absolutely unforgettable.

The villa prepared for us was stunning, offering a perfect blend of comfort, charm, and a breathtaking atmosphere. One of the most memorable highlights was the romantic candlelight dinner in the garden, beautifully set up with twinkling lights and a cozy bonfire. The ambiance was intimate and magical, making our celebration feel incredibly special.

We had brought our own raw ingredients for a cheese and charcuterie plate, and to our delight, Erin, the incredible manager, offered to prepare it beautifully for us. It was such a thoughtful gesture that added an extra touch of elegance to our evening. The in-house birthday cake was another delightful surprise, not only beautifully presented but also absolutely delicious!

Another highlight of our stay was the immaculate pool—so clean and well-maintained that I didn’t want to get out, even when it started raining! Having the entire pool to myself made for an incredibly serene and relaxing experience.

A special thank you to Manager Erin from Malaysia, who went above and beyond in organizing every detail to perfection. Her warmth, attentiveness, and genuine hospitality made our stay truly unforgettable. We are deeply grateful for the effort she and the entire Balibo Fort Hotel team, now managed by Pelikan Paradise, put into making our celebration so special.

If you’re looking for a place that combines history, beauty, and world-class hospitality, Balibo Fort Hotel is a must-visit. We will cherish these memories forever and can’t wait to return!

Highly Recommended!

With gratitude,
Kivo & Flora

review_text: Great for adventure seekers who want to get away from it all. However, you can buy a fish from the local fishermen, and for a small fee they will cook it for you.  You can build a campfire on the beach.  At low tide, there are lots of rocks.  It isn't a great swimming/snorkeling beach.  For that, either hike south near the fishing boats or go to Jaco Island itself.  We had the place to ourselves for 2 nights, but then on the third a bunch of youth on motorbikes showed up and rudely played their music very loud late into the night then again in the morning.  The co-op (village) runs the place.  They rotate workers each week, so you never know who you will get.  All in all, its remoteness, natural beauty, fascinating caves, and exquisite marine environment makes it well worth the effort.  Just come prepared  as if you were camping just in case.  No credit cards are accepted here.

review_text:
One of Timor Leste’s two islands (with Atauro Island), Jaco is an uninhabited, 10km2 island about 700m off the eastern end of mainland Timor-Leste, home to beautifully clear waters off a white sand beach. There isn’t really anything on the island, other than an impressive set of whale bones to the south of where the boats land, and a thick bush interior with no paths, but it is a quiet and relaxing place. Just off shore are several patches of coral, though less diverse or life filled than those around Atauro Island, and with stronger currents. It isn’t possible to hire snorkel gear locally so bring it with you. There are a surprising number of deer, given that there is no reliable fresh water supply on the island. Crocodiles are regularly spotted by Valu Beach so it is advisable to stay out of the water. The strong currents deter, but not entirely, crocodiles from visiting Jaco Island. There have been no publicised fatalities but near misses have happened, so enter the water at your own risk.

Finally the staff of Maddog were outstanding. All, from drivers to guides, were extremely professional and competent in their job.  Everything was always set up to schedule and ran very smoothly. Highly recommend for a once in a lifetime experience!

review_text:
We stayed here on three separate occasions during our time in TL. Every time was a pleasure. And we actively looked forward to returning here.

The staff are absolutely amazing and friendly. They will do their best to help.

The Filipina receptionists are efficient and welcoming. They will gladly keep any luggage you don’t need safely for your return.

Responses to arrange airport pick up are very quick. They were always very prompt.

If you need to leave early, they will bring a packed hot cooked breakfast to your room on time.

We had a problem with air conditioning in our room one night and were told the maintenance staff had gone home (understandably). Lo and behold at 9:30 PM they actually came to fix the problem so that we could sleep well in Dili’s  heat. Truly remarkable.

Breakfast is a cooked breakfast with beautifully cooked eggs and beans. Plus fruit. Fresh fruit juices are also available for an extra fee.

We were two but had booked the two bedroom ground floor apartment for our stays. WOW! Huge with one double bed and two twins and two bathrooms plus kitchenette. We even had a handy washer and dryer.(You can buy washing powder at the little convenience stores almost across the street from the hotel). Everything was very clean, water was hot, and the WIFI worked well.

There a decent bakery/cafe  a five minute walk from the hotel and lots of coconut and fresh produce vendors nearby.

The hotel was a small pool.

The only suggested improvement would be to have their shuttle available to guests for short hops across town for a fee like some other hotels in Dili offer, given that it takes so long to get a local taxi. (Microlet taxi bus services are easily available from close to the hotel if need be.)

review_text:
Highly Recommend Arbiru Beach Resort!

I’ve stayed at quite a few hotels around Timor-Leste, and while many of them look new and modern, I still prefer Arbiru Beach Resort when it comes to overall value and service.

Check-in was quick and smooth. I originally asked to pay by card, but they kindly explained that credit cards aren’t commonly used in Timor-Leste, and only one bank accepts them with high fees. The hotel doesn’t work with that bank, so they only accept cash. Just a heads up make sure to bring enough cash with you!

My stay was great overall. The staff were super friendly and helpful, the food was delicious, the pool was lovely, the Wi-Fi was fast, and my room was spacious and comfortable. The breakfast team was especially attentive, always checking in to see if I needed anything.

The resort itself isn’t brand new and could use a bit of work on the outside, but the rooms were spotless, nicely painted, and cleaned daily. Laundry service was also included in the room rate, which was a nice bonus.

They also offered free airport pickup and drop-off, which saved me $30 total (since taxis here cost about $15 each way). Prices in Timor are higher than in Bali, but after a few days, I understood why almost everything has to be imported.

Honestly, I feel like this hotel has so much potential. If tourism in Timor picks up, I think Arbiru could be truly amazing. For now, it’s already a fantastic place to stay, especially if you’re looking for comfort, great service, and a relaxing vibe.

review_text:
Walking into Timor Plaza today, I see a modern building with glass elevators and bright lights. It feels like any shopping mall you would find in other Asian cities. But this place carries a heavy story. It opened in October 2011 as the first modern shopping center in Timor-Leste. It was built by the Jape Group, a family business started by Jape Kong Su, a man born in Balibo who fled the country in 1975 and built his fortune in Darwin, Australia. He returned in 1999 to help rebuild his homeland, and this mall became his biggest project.

Today, the place is busy. The Jape family says more than 3,000 people work in the Dili Central compound every day, directly or indirectly. The mall has a supermarket, banks, phone companies, restaurants, and the only cinema in the country. There is even a free medical clinic run by the Order of Malta. For many Timorese, it is a place to find work, buy goods, or watch a movie. For others, it is a symbol that their country is moving forward.

The founder passed away in 2022, but the Jape family still owns and runs the mall. They plan to expand the compound to more buildings, making it a bigger commercial center for Dili. The mall is a place of progress and business. It is also a place that reminds me of the struggles that came with building it. Both things are true at the same time.

위생 상태가 의심되는 상황에서 교환을 요청했지만, 스무디만 바꿔주고 주스는 문제가 없다며 그대로 다시 내주었습니다. 이미 이물질이 나온 음료를 휘저어서 다시 마시라는 대응은 도저히 납득할 수 없습니다.

이후에도 상황은 더 심각했습니다.
2시간이 지나서야 짬뽕이 나오고, 2시간 30분 후에 탕수육이 나왔습니다. 그런데 그 시점에서 갑자기 연어초밥과 비빔밥은 제공이 불가능하다고 통보했습니다.

가장 충격적인 건 사장님의 태도였습니다.
이 정도 문제 상황이면 직접 나와 사과하고 설명하는 것이 최소한의 책임이라고 생각합니다. 하지만 직원들 뒤에 숨어 대응을 피했고, 사장님과의 대화를 요청하자 “없다”는 말만 반복했습니다.

그런데 실제로는 매장 안에서 이어폰을 끼고 휴대폰을 하고 있었습니다. 손님을 기만하는 수준의 대응입니다.

위생, 서비스, 책임감 모두 최악입니다.

Our first visit is definitely one for the books. It was one of those unplanned date nights with my husband—after attending a workshop that ended late, we found ourselves hungry at around 9:20 PM. Despite being near the end of their operating hours, the team welcomed us with warm smiles and great hospitality.

We were seated right away with no waiting time, and it was a plus that there’s parking available with a security guard. The menu was promptly given, and within about 10 minutes, our food was already served—sirloin steak with rice, samgyeopsal, beef bulgogi, miso soup, and iced honey lemon (which was incredibly refreshing!).

The food itself was truly remarkable. The miso soup tasted authentic and comforting—like a warm hug, perfectly paired with the cool sea breeze. The pork and beef were tender and flavorful, and even the rice stood out—you can tell it’s the kind Koreans use, cooked perfectly.

We finished everything in about 20 minutes—not just because we were hungry, but because the food was genuinely satisfying and comforting. Even my husband, who follows a low-carb diet, really enjoyed the meal (I happily took care of the rice!). And the radish kimchi? Absolutely perfect.

While the price is a bit on the higher side, it’s definitely value for money. Considering the availability of parking, security, authentic Korean ingredients, and overall quality, it’s understandable—especially since many items are imported to achieve that true taste. They clearly don’t skimp on ingredients.

Plus, they also have a Korean supermarket downstairs, which makes the whole experience even better. I’d definitely love to come back with my kids next time and try more items on the menu—I honestly want to try them all.

I’m still daydreaming about all the food we ate until now.

Overall, a memorable experience with great food, excellent service, and a welcoming atmosphere. We’ll definitely be back.

I will be returning here again and again.

Mixed experience staying two nights at Baguia Fort. The fort is incredibly atmospheric, and has great views of the surrounding landscape. Our room was in one of the standalone buildings, with two comfortable double beds, and an en-suite (though a few maintenance issues).

The rate was $25 per person for bed and breakfast (egg rolls). Additional meals were reasonable at $5 though of the 5 meals we ate there 4 turned up at least half an hour later than confirmed...

Information on hiking Matebian (the second highest mountain in Timor-Leste) was surprisingly inaccurate, dangerously so, given that is the main attraction in the area.

We drove up to the village of Waiboro, along the worst road I've driven in 2,000km of motorbike riding around Timor-Leste. It was barely passable, and would need a local driver with a decent 4WD or people with good off-road motorbike skills to navigate.

From here it is a relentless 1,100m ascent to the summit of Matebian, with almost no shade. Expect to take 3-5 hours to reach the summit, and another 2-4 hours to descend the way you came. A local guide (helpfully organised by Baguia Fort) is essential as there are large stretches with no clear path.

Starting from Baguia Fort would involve an additional 800m of ascent and descent.

It's an incredible place to visit and stay, but please take into account the information above. Matebian is a rewarding but tough mountain to summit (and drive to reach!).

review_text:
Forte da Baguia foi um forte Português construído na cidade de Baguia, Baucau,Timor-Leste, durante o governo de José Celestino da Silva (1894 – 1908).

O forte foi construído com um muro de duas camadas, sendo uma externa e a outra interna que o envolve no formato de um retângulo no qual existem três edifícios ao todo. Nos cantos da parede há duas torres e entre elas uma abertura. Envolvendo a parede interna há mais um muro de defesa, que utiliza a encosta como proteção adicional e também uma ponte sobre um fosso na sua frente.

Durante a rebelião de Viqueque, no início de junho de 1959, os insurgentes tentaram tomar o forte.eles contavam com pelo menos cem rebeldes, no entanto, foram repelidos por soldados profissionais, que contavam com um uso mais efetivo dos equipamentos bélicos e também tinham uma metralhadora como aliada. Esta tentativa fracassada de tomar o forte resultou em destruição de grande parte do forte.

O forte foi reinaugurado em 2014, na sua cerimonia de reinauguração contou com a presença de políticos e cidadãos ilustres dentre eles Manuel Gonçalves de Jesus (Embaixador português) Dra. Maria Isabel de Jesus Ximenes (Ministra do turismo) e Dr. António Guterres (Presidente do Município de Baucau), Atualmente o forte funcionam como um albergue.

Foodie Critique: Joyful Restaurant (Timor Plaza)

Stopped by this Hong Kong–style restaurant around noon. With only two guests in the dining room—including myself—I expected at least a smile or a welcome. Instead, there was silence and stares. Even getting a menu required me to ask, which set the tone for the meal.

I had come looking forward to a proper Hong Kong–style milk tea, but surprisingly it wasn’t available. Only bubble tea was offered, which I declined. For a restaurant positioned as HK-style, not having this basic staple is a gap.

I ordered the Bitter Melon Beef Rice. Unfortunately, the beef was overly salty, and the bitter melon lacked balance. The only part I can compliment was the plain white rice, which at least helped tone down the saltiness of the dish.

Reflections:
•	When the restaurant is quiet, acknowledging and welcoming every guest is essential.
•	Service should be proactive, not reactive.
•	Food quality needs to reflect the promise of the cuisine—staples should be executed well, and flavors balanced.

There’s potential, but at present, the experience doesn’t live up to the concept. With stronger focus on service and more care in food execution, Joyful could move closer to delivering the true Hong Kong café experience. I wish the team well and hope they can elevate both hospitality and quality.

review_text:
Pura Giri Natha Dili is Timor Leste’s largest Balinese Hindu temple, located in the Taibesi area on the southern outskirts of Dili. It was built in 1987 during the Indonesian administration for Balinese Hindu immigrants and Indonesian soldiers. The temple was inaugurated on June 27, 1987, by Governor Mário Viegas Carrascalão. After Timor Leste became independent in 1999, most Hindus left the country, and by 2015, only 272 Hindus were recorded in the national census. The temple later fell into serious disrepair and was also damaged during the violence in 1999 and the internal conflict in 2006.

Restoration of the temple is now underway. In 2021, the Timor Leste government allocated about US$1.2 million for its reconstruction, with additional support from the Udayana University Timor Leste Alumni Association. By January 2023, the restoration was reported to be about 90 percent complete. Today, the temple is being developed not only as a place of worship but also as a cultural and spiritual tourism site. It serves Indonesians, Hindus from Nepal and India, and some local Timorese converts. For visitors, it is a unique sight: traditional Balinese Hindu architecture standing on a small hill in Dili, a city where the large majority of people are Catholic.

review_text:
When Timor Leste was occupied by Indonesia, this beach was known as "Pantai pasir putih" in Bahasa Indonesia, or "White sand beach". The name is appropriate - although not particularly imaginative - as the beach is covered in white sand!

When I visited, some 23 years ago, the beach was quite eerie. It was deserted, apart from myself, and there were little concrete picnic shelters dotted along the beach that were slowly filling with drifting sand or become overgrown with trees. There were also some old, decrepit "pedalo" boats, little boats that you can pedal in calm water, that were half-buried in the sand. Clearly, the shelters and pedal-boats dated from the 1970s, some twenty years earlier, when East Timor was a Portuguese colony and a popular destination for Portuguese holiday-makers.

It would be interesting to know if any of the old, decrepit concrete picnic shelters, or any other trace of its old history, still remain.

Anfahrt mit Roller möglich, aber schon eine Herausforderung. Gerade nach Regen ist die Piste sehr schlammig. Teils so tiefe Pfützen, dass man nur Barfuß durchkommt oder eben mit dem Roller. Auf dem Weg etliche Stände mit Getränken und Suppen. Beim Wandern leben die Teenies ihre Jugendkultur voll aus, hören laute Musik, schreien herum, werfen ihren Müll in die Natur. Ich hab mehrere Tüten davon aufgesammelt, aber da liegt leider noch genug herum. Gottes Schöpfung wird hier völlig missachtet. Ganz anderes Bild am Gipfel. An der Marienstatue wird gebeten und dem Herren gelobt. Alle sind leise und ehrfürchtig. Es ist ein Wallfahrtsort.
Es war schön zu sehen, dass so viele junge Leute Bergsteigen gehen. Die meisten sehr freundlich. Als einziger Europäischer bin ich auf viel Begeisterung gestoßen. Ist sicherlich nicht jedermanns Sache, aber ich vermute, dass es unter der Woche ruhiger ist.
Insgesamt lohnend, aber das mit dem vielen Müll und Lärm ist sehr traurig. Überlegt euch bitte wie sich Jesus oder Maria hier verhalten hätten. Ich bin mir sicher, dass sie diesen Müll und Abfall am Berg nicht gut gefunden hätten.

review_text:
For an independent traveler get a minitruck (3$)from Taibesi station in Dili. Look for the name „Hatu Builico“ on the trucks. From my understanding there’s a truck at a specific date and time that goes directly to Hatu Builico, the village near the summit. If it doesn’t (that happened to me) tell the driver you‘ll go to Mt. Ramelau. He‘ll drop you at the place called „Fleixa“ about 8 km after Maubisse. There‘s a sign „Mt. Ramelau“ pointing to a very bad unpaved road on the right. If you walk on this road, it‘s 18 km to Hatu Builico. The road is very scenic. In my case I met a villager from Hatu Builico and I just walked with him. He used cow paths and walked in straight line from Fleixa to Hatu Builico. This reduces the distance and took me only 2 hours to reach Hatu Builico but I wouldn’t attempt this if I was alone.
In Hatu Builico the villagers are very nice and friendly. Some can speak English and can help you find a hotel. From the village it‘s straightforward 4 km to the trail entrance and another 4 km to the summit.
If 18 km walking back to Fleixa doesn’t appeal to you, your hotel can arrange a transport either motorbike or 4WD for you. I paid 30$ for a ride with a motorbike to Maubisse.
